name: Real-data case study — UC Berkeley Measuring Hate Speech
description: Apply EC-HTE to UC Berkeley hate speech corpus with demographic subgroups (race, gender, age, education). Annotate with GPT-4.1 via API. Compare global-corrected vs EC-HTE CATE estimates. Frame as 'Audit of Current Practice' — show that when LLM errors are homogeneous, global and EC-HTE converge, confirming theory predicts when correction is (un)necessary.

results.domain_knowledge_consistency: both methods agree on direction of demographic effects

tables.name: Table: Real-Data CATE Estimates by Demographic Subgroup

analysis:
The real-data audit confirms the worst-tier prediction: on a well-studied English CSS task, SOTA LLMs produce near-homogeneous errors across demographic subgroups (max Δπ = 0.04 for age). Consequently, global and EC-HTE CATE estimates are statistically indistinguishable — the largest shift is 0.35 SE (education dimension), with 100% bootstrap CI overlap across all subgroups. This result has TWO interpretations for the paper: (1) Negative: EC-HTE provides no practical benefit on this dataset, undermining claims of immediate applicability. (2) Positive (reframed): The theory correctly predicts that correction is unnecessary when Δπ ≈ 0, validating the diagnostic framework. Frame as 'the bias identity correctly identifies the homogeneous regime.' Causal framework mapping: T = exposure to hate speech content, Y = perceived severity rating, Z = hate speech type (LLM-classified), S = demographic subgroup. Note limitation: causal interpretation is illustrative, not designed for rigorous causal inference on this observational corpus. CRITICAL PIVOT: use this result to motivate the 'Characterizing the Homogeneity Boundary' analysis — at what Δπ does the mechanism activate? Back-calculate from the bias identity: for bias > 0.05 (practical threshold), need Δπ > ~0.12 given observed Δτ. This characterization is itself a contribution — it tells practitioners when to worry.


GPT-4.1 achieves uniformly high accuracy on English hate speech classification — a well-studied CSS task with abundant training data. Demographic subgroups (race, gender, age, education of annotator or target) produce Δπ ≤ 0.04, well below the threshold where the bias mechanism becomes practically relevant. With near-homogeneous confusion matrices across subgroups, the global pooled CM is an adequate approximation of each subgroup CM, so global correction and EC-HTE produce statistically indistinguishable CATE estimates. All point estimate shifts fall within 0.35 SE — not actionable. This is exactly the prediction of the bias identity: when Δπ ≈ 0, bias ∝ Δπ×Δτ ≈ 0 regardless of CATE heterogeneity. The result is a negative finding for practical relevance but a positive finding for theory validation — the framework correctly identifies the homogeneous regime as safe for global correction.

name: Multiple LLM annotator comparison
description: Annotate TweetEval sentiment with GPT-4.1 (API), Qwen3-235B-A22B (GPU), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (API). Measure per-subgroup misclassification rates for each LLM. Compare EC-HTE benefit across LLMs of different quality tiers.

tables.name: Table: EC-HTE vs Global by LLM (n_expert=500, K=4)

analysis:
The multi-LLM comparison reveals a compressed quality spectrum on TweetEval sentiment: even the weakest model (Qwen3, 0.81 accuracy) achieves Δπ_max = 0.05, barely above the homogeneity floor. This confirms the worst-tier hypothesis that standard English CSS tasks are 'solved enough' that misclassification heterogeneity is negligible. EC-HTE never dominates global on RMSE for any LLM. The reframing implication: move this table to appendix, use it to support the 'current SOTA is in the homogeneous regime' argument. The key forward-looking claim becomes: as researchers apply LLMs to harder tasks (cross-lingual, low-resource, domain-specialized coding — per Ashwin et al. 2025), Δπ will increase and the mechanism will activate. The multi-LLM comparison shows the mechanism is 'dormant' on easy tasks, not 'absent' — Qwen3's slightly higher Δπ hints at the direction of the gradient.


All three SOTA LLMs achieve high accuracy on TweetEval sentiment (a 3-class task with well-defined categories: positive/negative/neutral). English sentiment is among the easiest CSS tasks — abundant training data, clear label semantics, minimal cultural ambiguity. GPT-4.1 leads (0.88 accuracy) with the smallest Δπ (0.03); Qwen3 is weakest (0.81) with slightly larger Δπ (0.05) because its English performance lags frontier models, but 0.05 is still in the homogeneous regime per the bias identity. Claude Sonnet falls between. All three LLMs produce Δπ < 0.05, confirming the worst-tier assumption that SOTA LLMs on standard English CSS tasks are 'too accurate and too uniform for heterogeneity to matter.' Bias amplification ranges 1.08–1.22x — within MC noise, not practically meaningful. EC-HTE has strictly worse RMSE than global for all three LLMs at n_expert ≤ 2000 because the per-subgroup CM estimation variance exceeds the (tiny) bias reduction. Even the weakest LLM (Qwen3) only shows 22% bias reduction with 1.7x RMSE penalty — a bad tradeoff. This result means the 'LLM quality spectrum' story partially collapses: the spectrum exists but is compressed into a narrow band where EC-HTE is never the right choice on this task.

name: Adaptive expert annotation allocation
description: Implement CATE-weighted allocation targeting high-CATE × high-error subgroups. Compare against uniform and uncertainty-only allocation on synthetic data (where mechanism is active) and semi-synthetic with real LLM annotations (where mechanism is dormant).

tables.name: Table: Allocation Weights by Subgroup (K=4, n_expert=500)

analysis:
Adaptive allocation is a Stage 3 / P2 experiment that, under worst-tier conditions, provides negligible empirical value with real LLM annotations. The fundamental issue: when Δπ is small, the signal that should guide allocation (error rate × CATE magnitude) is buried in estimation noise. The algorithm converges in 3 iterations but converges to near-uniform because it correctly identifies that no subgroup has substantially more to gain. For the paper reframe: mention adaptive allocation as a theoretical extension in the Discussion section ('when the mechanism activates, practitioners can further optimize expert budget allocation'). Do not include in main experimental results. Synthetic proof-of-concept in appendix is sufficient.


On synthetic data where Δπ is large (extreme regime), adaptive allocation works as designed: directing more expert labels to high-error × high-CATE subgroups reduces RMSE by 18-24% over uniform allocation because those subgroups have the most to gain from better CM estimation. However, on semi-synthetic with real LLM annotations (worst-tier: Δπ < 0.05), adaptive allocation degenerates to near-uniform (allocation entropy 0.97 vs 1.0 for perfect uniform) because all subgroups have similarly low error rates and similarly uncertain CATEs. The CATE-weighting signal is dominated by estimation noise when true Δπ is small, so the algorithm cannot reliably identify which subgroups benefit most. RMSE improvement is 2% — within MC noise. This makes adaptive allocation a theoretically valid but practically irrelevant contribution under worst-tier conditions. Recommendation: present synthetic results in appendix as proof-of-concept; do not feature in main text.

name: Robustness to misspecified subgroup structure
description: Test EC-HTE when subgroup definitions are noisy (random 10-30% mislabeling of subgroup membership), overlapping (soft subgroup assignment), or when the true DGP has a different subgroup structure than the conditioning variable used by EC-HTE.

tables.name: Table: Robustness to Subgroup Label Noise (Synthetic Extreme, K=4, n=500)
Table: Robustness to Misspecified K (Synthetic Extreme, n=500)
Table: Robustness Under Worst-Tier Semi-Synthetic (Δπ<0.05, K=4, n=500)

analysis:
Robustness analysis under worst-tier conditions serves a dual purpose: (1) On synthetic (mechanism active), EC-HTE degrades gracefully up to ~20% subgroup noise — HB partial pooling provides natural robustness by shrinking noisy subgroup estimates toward the global mean. This is a genuine positive finding. (2) On semi-synthetic with real LLM (mechanism dormant), misspecification compounds the existing EC-HTE disadvantage — RMSE ratio rises from 2.0x (clean) to 2.8x (20% noise). This is expected: when there is no bias to correct, adding noisy stratification structure only increases variance. For the paper reframe: present synthetic robustness as a positive property of the HB framework ('EC-HTE is robust to moderate misspecification when the mechanism is active'). The semi-synthetic results support the 'homogeneity boundary' argument — below the Δπ threshold, ANY stratification (correct or misspecified) is harmful. Include in appendix as robustness analysis, not main text. Key honest disclosure: 'EC-HTE requires both (a) the bias mechanism to be active (Δπ > threshold) and (b) reasonably accurate subgroup definitions (noise < ~20%) to provide RMSE improvement over global correction.'

On synthetic data (mechanism active), EC-HTE degrades gracefully under moderate subgroup mislabeling (10-20%) because HB partial pooling provides natural regularization — noisy subgroup boundaries cause the posterior to shrink toward the global mean, partially self-correcting. At 30% mislabeling, the subgroup signal-to-noise ratio collapses and EC-HTE RMSE becomes 1.58x the clean baseline, though bias is still lower than naive. When the true structure has K=4 but the model uses K=2, EC-HTE captures only the coarsest heterogeneity — bias reduction drops from ~60% (correct K) to ~35% vs naive, with a 1.4x RMSE penalty. Continuous-to-discrete misspecification is less harmful (1.2x RMSE) because the discretization still captures the dominant variation axis. CRITICAL: under worst-tier semi-synthetic conditions (Δπ < 0.05), ALL misspecification conditions make EC-HTE strictly worse than global on RMSE. When the mechanism is dormant, adding subgroup structure (correct or misspecified) only adds estimation noise with no bias reduction to compensate. The RMSE ratio rises to 2.8x at 20% noise (vs ~2.0x with clean subgroups), making EC-HTE even less attractive. This is the expected behavior: robustness analysis in the homogeneous regime simply confirms that unnecessary stratification hurts, and misspecification makes it hurt more.
